title: Fourier transform, DFT, windowing, and the STFT
summary: Explain how the transform comes from the series, read the DFT formula and compute bin spacing, say why a windowed tone leaks and why tapering helps, and compute every STFT parameter from Fₛ, frame size and shift — the Lab 7/8 skill.
sourceNote: fourier_transform.pdf, dft.pdf, windowing.pdf, stft.pdf (Koo's notes/slides), J&M (2008) §9.3.2, NI 'Understanding FFTs and Windowing', Labs 5–7.

sections.heading: From series to transform: let the period go to infinity

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Speech isn't periodic** The Fourier series needs a periodic signal — it only has ingredients at multiples of F₀. A whole sentence isn't periodic. Koo's move (fourier_transform.pdf §2): take a T₀-long chunk of any signal, pretend it repeats every T₀ (so it has a series), then let T₀ grow without limit. As T₀ → ∞ the repeats move infinitely far apart — you're left with the original signal — and F₀ = 1/T₀ → 0, so the harmonics kF₀ crowd together into a **continuous** frequency axis. ==The sum becomes an integral==. That integral is the Fourier transform.

blocks.title: Same shape as the series formulas, with ∫ dF replacing Σ over k and X_F (a function of continuous F) replacing X_k. Opposite signs in the exponents; no normalizing factor under this convention.
blocks.body:
Fourier transform:          X_F = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} x(t) · e^{−j2πFt} dt      "how much of frequency F is in x"
Inverse Fourier transform:  x(t) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} X_F · e^{j2πFt} dF      "rebuild x from all its frequencies"

blocks.title: Where X_F comes from
blocks.body:
Turn X_k and the series into X_F and the integral.

1. Start from the series x(t) = Σ X_k e^{j2πF_k t} with F_k = kF₀, and the coefficient formula X_k = (1/T₀)∫ x(t)e^{−j2πF_k t} dt over one period.
2. Multiply each series term by F₀/F₀: x(t) = Σ (X_k/F₀) e^{j2πF_k t} · F₀. Now it looks like a Riemann sum — rectangles of width ΔF = F₀ and height (X_k/F₀)e^{j2πF_k t}.
3. Define X_F as the limit of X_k/F₀ as F₀ → 0 and F_k → F. The Riemann sum becomes ∫ X_F e^{j2πFt} dF: the inverse transform.
4. For X_F itself: since 1/T₀ = F₀, X_k/F₀ = ∫_{−T₀/2}^{T₀/2} x(t)e^{−j2πF_k t} dt. Let T₀ → ∞: the limits go to ±∞, F_k → F, and the left side is X_F. That's the forward transform.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** The transform is the load-bearing math of an absurd amount of technology: MRI scanners record raw data in the frequency domain and inverse-transform it into images; JPEG compresses photos with the DCT, a close cousin, keeping the low spatial frequencies your eye actually notices; EQ and noise reduction are 'transform, edit X_F, transform back'. ==When an engineer says 'in the frequency domain', this pair of integrals is the door they walked through== — and in speech, everything from here to ASR lives on the other side of it.

sections.heading: Making it computable: DTFT and DFT

blocks.md: Computers can't integrate over continuous time or evaluate a continuum of frequencies. So we discretize twice more (dft.pdf). **Time**: sample at Fₛ (Chapter 3's move), x[n] = x(n/Fₛ), and the ∫…dt becomes a sum over samples. **Frequency**: for an N-sample signal, evaluate at just N equally spaced frequencies. ==Two discretizations, two names==: discrete time only → DTFT; discrete time *and* frequency → DFT, the thing computers actually run.

blocks.title: F̂ is frequency in cycles per SAMPLE (F/Fₛ). The DTFT is periodic in F̂ with period 1 because e^{j2π(F̂+1)n} = e^{j2πF̂n}·e^{j2πn} and e^{j2πn} = 1 for integer n. The DFT samples one period of it at N points.
blocks.body:
DTFT (discrete time, continuous F̂):
   X(F̂) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} x[n] e^{−j2πF̂n}                  F̂ = F/Fₛ, consider [−1/2, 1/2]

DFT (N samples in, N coefficients out):
   X[k] = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} x[n] e^{−j2π(k/N)n}               k = −N/2 … N/2−1   (F̂ = k/N)
   x[n] = (1/N) Σ_{k=−N/2}^{N/2−1} X[k] e^{j2π(k/N)n}      inverse DFT — exact, by orthogonality

bin k corresponds to frequency  F = k · Fₛ/N        bin spacing = Fₛ/N Hz

the spacing between DFT bins, in Hz. Where it comes from: N samples at rate Fₛ span N/Fₛ seconds; the DFT treats that span as one period, so its 'fundamental' is 1/(N/Fₛ) = Fₛ/N, and bin k sits at k·Fₛ/N. A longer frame (bigger N at fixed Fₛ) gives finer frequency spacing. This is the seed of the time–frequency trade-off at the end.

blocks.md:
- N samples in → N complex numbers out. Each X[k] is the complex amplitude (Chapter 4) of frequency k·Fₛ/N.
- k = N/2 is excluded because F̂ = 1/2 and F̂ = −1/2 are the same point (that's the Nyquist frequency, Chapter 3).
- The **FFT** is just a fast algorithm for computing the DFT. ==Same numbers, fewer operations==; fastest when N is a power of 2 — which is why frame sizes get zero-padded to 512, 1024, 2048.

**Where you'll meet this after the exam** The FFT has a serious claim to most-run algorithm on Earth: it's inside every audio codec, modem, radar, and the spectrogram view of every DAW. The bin arithmetic you just practiced is daily-driver knowledge — it's how you read the `librosa.stft` docs, choose `n_fft` so a mel filterbank has enough low-frequency bins, or explain why a guitar tuner needs a long buffer to separate 82.4 Hz from 87.3 Hz. ##Fₛ/N is the first number to compute whenever a spectrum looks wrong## — most 'mystery peaks' turn out to be two real peaks sharing one bin.

blocks.prompt: 512-point DFT of speech sampled at 16 kHz: bin spacing, and which bin holds 1 kHz?
You want 10 Hz resolution at Fₛ = 8 kHz. How many samples per frame, and how long is that frame?
blocks.answer: N = Fₛ/resolution = 800 samples; 800/8000 = 0.1 s = 100 ms. (Too long for speech — sounds change faster than that. The trade-off is real.)

blocks.md: To analyze a changing signal, cut it into short **frames** (a **sliding window**) and transform each one. But the DFT carries a hidden assumption: it treats each frame as one period of a wave that ==repeats forever== — whatever the frame's edges look like, the DFT sees them stitched end-to-end. That assumption is where the trouble starts.

blocks.title: A 100 Hz tone in a 25 ms rectangular window
blocks.body:
Why does the spectrum show energy at frequencies other than 100 Hz?

1. A 25 ms frame, repeated, has period 0.025 s, so the DFT's harmonic grid is F₀ = 1/0.025 = 40 Hz: 40, 80, 120, 160…
2. 100 Hz is **not on the grid** — it's not an integer multiple of 40. There's no single harmonic to hold it, so 'harmonics close to 100 Hz share the burden': energy smears into 80 and 120 Hz and beyond.
3. Second cause: 25 ms is 2.5 cycles of 100 Hz, so the frame ends mid-cycle. Repeating it creates a **sudden jump** at each seam. Sharp jumps need a broad band of frequencies to represent (think of the triangle wave's corners in Lab 4).
4. Together these are **spectral leakage**: a pure tone shows up as a smeared hump instead of a single line.

blocks.md: The fix: multiply the frame by a **window function** that fades in from zero and back out to zero — a **Hamming** or **Hann** window — instead of the abrupt **rectangular** window. ##No jump at the seams → far less leakage##. The cost (NI reading): the main peak gets a little wider, and you lose a little amplitude accuracy. For speech, always taper; Lab 7's notebook compares rectangular vs Hamming on the same tone.

blocks.caption: Left: rectangular window — the frame starts and stops abruptly, so its repeated copies jump at the seams. Right: Hamming window — the same frame faded in and out, so the seams meet at silence. The right one leaks far less. Hover any part.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** Every spectrum you will ever look at was windowed by *somebody*: Praat, Audacity's Plot Spectrum, and `scipy.signal.stft` all default to a taper, and the analyzer in your DAW has a window menu most users never open. Leakage is why a pure test tone grows 'skirts' in a plugin analyzer and why two close harmonics can smear into one blob. ==When a peak looks suspicious, ask what window made it== — engineers and phoneticians alike learn to distrust the spectrum before they distrust the signal.

blocks.prompt: A 440 Hz tone is analyzed with a 20 ms rectangular window. Will it leak? Which nearby bins get the energy?
blocks.answer: Grid F₀ = 1/0.02 = 50 Hz: 400, 450, 500… 440 isn't on it, and 20 ms is 8.8 cycles — ends mid-cycle. Yes, it leaks, mostly into the 400 and 450 Hz bins. A 25 ms window (grid 40 Hz: 440 = 11 × 40, and 11 whole cycles) would not leak at all — that's the special case.

blocks.body: Split the signal into (overlapping, tapered) frames and run an FFT on each. Stack the resulting spectra side by side over time → the **spectrogram**.

blocks.caption: The STFT, mechanically: a 25 ms window slides along the waveform in 10 ms hops, so neighboring frames overlap by 15 ms. Each colored frame is tapered, FFT'd, and becomes the same-colored column of the spectrogram below — time across, frequency up, shade = magnitude. Every spectrogram you've ever seen is exactly this stack of FFT columns. Hover any part.

rows: Length of each frame, in s or samples
usually = nperseg; > nperseg zero-pads; < nperseg is an error
one-sided has nfft//2 + 1 bins (k = 0 … N//2); fine for real signals
librosa: first frame starts at sample 0; scipy ShortTimeFFT: first frame is centered on sample 0

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why you can't have both** Frequency resolution is Fₛ/N: a **longer** window gives finer frequency detail. But a longer window blurs *when* things happen — ==sharp in time or sharp in frequency, never both at once==. **Short window (≈5 ms)** → high time resolution, coarse frequency → a **broad-band** spectrogram: you see each glottal pulse as a vertical striation and formants as wide dark bands. **Long window (≈25–50 ms)** → fine frequency, blurred time → a **narrow-band** spectrogram: you see the harmonics as thin horizontal lines. Phoneticians use broad-band to read formants and narrow-band to read pitch. This is the one conceptual question Day 8 is guaranteed to ask.

blocks.prompt: Fₛ = 8 kHz, frame 32 ms, shift 8 ms, 2 s of audio. nperseg, hop, noverlap, frames (no padding), one-sided bins if nfft = nperseg.
Which spectrogram shows harmonics as horizontal lines, and what produces it?
blocks.answer: Narrow-band, from a long analysis window (fine frequency resolution). A short window gives broad-band: vertical striations and formant bands instead.

blocks.body: Waveform → sample at Fₛ (Chapter 3) → cut into tapered frames (windowing) → DFT/FFT each frame (this chapter) → complex coefficients X[k], magnitude and phase per bin (Chapter 4) → stack over time = spectrogram (STFT). Everything after Day 10 (Mel, cepstrum, ASR) starts from that spectrogram.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** The 25 ms / 10 ms / 16 kHz setup in the stepper is, almost digit for digit, the front end of Whisper, wav2vec, wake-word detectors, and the MFCC pipeline in decades of ASR papers — ==when a paper says '80-dim log-mel features at 100 frames per second', you can now derive every number in that sentence== (100 fps IS the 10 ms hop). Spectrogram reading is a profession: forensic analysts compare speakers on STFTs in court, and clinicians track voice disorders on them. Even your phone's call noise suppression runs an STFT, edits the columns, and inverts it — a hundred times a second, in real time.

exercises.title: Bin spacing and what you can resolve
exercises.prompt: A 16 kHz recording; you take a DFT of N = 512 samples. (a) Bin spacing in Hz? (b) Which bin is closest to 1000 Hz? (c) Two vowel harmonics at 1000 and 1015 Hz — can this DFT tell them apart? (d) What N would you need to resolve them, and how long a frame is that in ms?
hints: Bin spacing = Fₛ/N. Bin k sits at k·Fₛ/N. To resolve two tones, the spacing must be smaller than their distance apart.
The error to avoid: thinking more samples per second helps resolution. Frequency resolution depends on the frame *length in seconds* (N/Fₛ) — longer frame, finer bins. Fₛ alone doesn't fix it.
Need Fₛ/N < 15 → N > 16000/15 ≈ 1067 → the next power of 2 is 2048. Frame length = N/Fₛ.
solution: (c) No — 15 Hz apart, bins are 31.25 Hz apart. They land in the same bin and smear together.
(d) N ≥ 1067; use N = 2048 → spacing 7.8 Hz. Frame = 2048/16000 = 128 ms — long enough that a vowel may have changed during it. That's the time–frequency trade-off.
exercises.why: Every spectrogram setting you'll ever choose is this calculation: narrow-band (long frames, see harmonics, blur time) versus wide-band (short frames, see formants and timing, blur frequency). Speech scientists pick by ear, but the ear is doing this arithmetic.

exercises.title: STFT parameters from scratch (Lab 7/8)
exercises.prompt: Fₛ = 16000 Hz, frame length 25 ms, frame shift 10 ms, 2 s of audio, FFT size = next power of 2 above the frame. Compute: samples per frame, samples per shift, FFT size N, bin spacing, number of frames, and the time between spectrogram columns.
hints: Convert every time to samples by multiplying by Fₛ: 0.025 × 16000 and 0.010 × 16000. FFT size is the next power of 2 above samples-per-frame.
The common error is using the FFT size (512) as the bin spacing denominator with the frame length in ms — keep units straight: spacing = Fₛ/N with N in samples.
Number of frames ≈ (total samples − frame) / shift + 1. Time between columns is just the shift, in seconds.
solution: N = 512 (next power of 2 above 400; the frame is zero-padded to 512).
exercises.why: These exact numbers — 25 ms window, 10 ms hop, 16 kHz — are the defaults in nearly every speech recognizer ever built, including the ones on your phone. Being able to derive them means you can read any ASR paper's preprocessing section and know what the model actually sees.

exercises.title: Why the peak smears, and what the window does
exercises.prompt: You DFT a pure 1000 Hz tone with N = 512 at Fₛ = 16 kHz and see a clean single peak. You change the tone to 1010 Hz and the peak turns into a smear with skirts. Explain why, and say what applying a Hamming window before the DFT changes — both the good and the bad.

choices.text: 1010 Hz is above Nyquist, so it aliases
choices.feedback: Nyquist is 8000 Hz; 1010 is nowhere near it. This is about bins, not aliasing.

choices.text: 1010 Hz doesn't land on a bin (bins are 31.25 Hz apart), so the frame doesn't contain a whole number of cycles; the rectangular cut-off creates a jump at the edges, which spreads energy into neighbouring bins
choices.feedback: Right. That spread is spectral leakage, and it comes from the abrupt edges of the rectangular window.

choices.text: The DFT can only represent frequencies that are multiples of 1000
choices.feedback: It represents multiples of Fₛ/N = 31.25 Hz. 1000 happens to be one (bin 32); 1010 isn't.

hints: Check whether 1010 is a multiple of the bin spacing 31.25. If not, the frame holds a non-integer number of cycles — what does the start and end of the frame look like then?
The error is blaming aliasing or the tone itself. The tone is fine; the *cut* is the problem. A rectangular window chops the wave mid-cycle, and a sharp jump needs many frequencies to describe.
A Hamming window fades the frame in and out, removing the jump: the skirts drop dramatically. The cost: the main peak gets wider (about twice as wide), so two close tones are harder to separate.
solution: Bins are at multiples of 31.25 Hz. 1000 = 32 bins exactly; 1010 is not on a bin, so the 512-sample frame doesn't contain a whole number of cycles.
A rectangular window then cuts the wave mid-cycle. The discontinuity at the frame edges is a sharp feature, and sharp features spread across many frequencies — leakage: a smeared peak with sidelobes.
Hamming windowing tapers the frame to zero at both ends, so there's no jump: sidelobes fall by tens of dB. Trade-off: the main lobe widens, so frequency resolution gets slightly worse.
That's why Lab 7's spectra with Hamming look 'cleaner but fatter'.
exercises.why: Every spectrogram you'll ever see was windowed, and the choice of window decides whether you're looking at real harmonics or at artifacts of the cut. Knowing the trade-off is what lets you distrust a peak that shouldn't be there.
